articles.title: The Biggest Victims Of Trump’s Economic D-Day On Iran
articles.summary: China represents Washington’s biggest test, buying more than 80% of Iran’s seaborne crude, while sanctions against major Chinese banks could trigger signific...
articles.body:
Trump's "economic D-Day" against Iran is built around one of Washington's most powerful weapons: access to the U.S. financial system. The problem is that the deeper Washington pushes into Iran's remaining trade, the bigger the targets become.

China buys more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude. Iraq relies on Iranian gas for as much as 40% of its electricity generation. Turkey imported 4.5 bcm of Iranian gas in the first half of this year, while India still maintains a heavily one-sided trade relationship with Tehran. The UAE, once one of Iran's most important commercial and financial conduits, has already suspended dealings with Tehran.

The U.S. Treasury can sanction tankers, traders and small Chinese refiners without creating much collateral damage outside the Iranian trade. Going after the major banks financing that commerce is different, however. The same is true of forcing Baghdad to choose between complying with Washington and keeping Iranian gas flowing to Iraqi power stations.

The Trump administration took a cautious approach on Monday. Its first round targeted nearly 60 individuals, companies and vessels and expanded sanctions across shipping, aviation, technology, gold and digital assets, but left China's major banks untouched.

That leaves the most powerful part of Trump's threat still hanging over Iran's trading partners. If the first round fails to cut Iranian commerce sufficiently, Washington can move from sanctioning the networks built to evade U.S. restrictions to targeting the banks and companies that still have substantial business to lose in the United States.

Here are five countries facing some of the hardest choices under Trump's new economic offensive against Iran.

No country buys more Iranian oil than China, making Beijing the largest remaining source of hard-currency revenue for Tehran. Chinese imports reached 1.58 million barrels per day earlier this year before the war and U.S. blockade began squeezing those flows, with shipments falling to roughly 534,000 bpd so far in August from 823,000 bpd in July, according to Reuters .

But China has spent years building an oil trade with Iran designed to minimize its exposure to U.S. sanctions. Independent teapot refineries buy much of the crude, tankers use ship-to-ship transfers and other methods to disguise its origin, and transactions are settled in Chinese currency through difficult-to-track intermediaries. Washington has repeatedly targeted pieces of that network, including Chinese refiners, trading companies and vessels involved.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln headed for port in Thailand after 250 days at sea
articles.summary: Sailors and crew members on the USS Abraham Lincoln, which recently departed the Middle East after being stationed in the region as part of the U.S. conflict with Iran, have a port call scheduled after 250 days at sea, USA Today reported Monday, citing family members. Texts to the outlet said the Lincoln planned to…
articles.body:
Sailors and crew members on the USS Abraham Lincoln, which recently departed the Middle East after being stationed in the region as part of the U.S. conflict with Iran, have a port call scheduled after 250 days at sea, USA Today reported Monday , citing family members.

Texts to the outlet said the Lincoln planned to stop in Thailand in early September after its extended deployment. One sailor told a relative to send hotel ideas that looked good in Thailand, while another told her family member that she was excited after having talked about visiting Thailand.

The Hill has reached out to the U.S. Navy for comment.

Reports of the port call came days after the USS George Washington, the aircraft carrier intended to relieve the Lincoln, arrived in the Middle East , leaving the U.S. without a carrier in Asia.

Multiple media reports noted deteriorating conditions aboard the Lincoln in the weeks leading up to its departure from the Middle East, including rotting food and mental health concerns among crew members.

Family members of those aboard said they received urgent messages about food and water shortages and mental health issues serious enough that several sailors attempted to jump overboard.

The aircraft carrier departed San Diego in November. The strike group was originally intended to return home in May but was redirected to the Middle East in January ahead of the Iran war, and it was deployed for more than 260 days — including more than 200 consecutive days without a port call.

Most of the Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee have called for a hearing with Pentagon leadership to discuss the impact of extended deployments in support of the Iran war on U.S. service members, including on the Lincoln.

“Recent reports of sailors suffering from severe mental health issues amid deteriorating conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln have only added to a disturbing pattern of failures to adequately plan and support our troops, who have been away from their families indefinitely as the Iran War drags on,” Democratic Senators wrote in a letter to committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.).

President Trump and other administration officials have dismissed reports about conditions on the Lincoln, claiming them to be false.

The conflict with Iran has been locked in a stalemate, with the Trump administration announcing new sanctions of a scale and severity akin to the U.S. landing on Normandy Beach during World War II, calling the new economic warfare on Iran “Economic D-Day.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday issued a global warning for countries to cut any financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system.

articles.title: Adiós al Código 78: la DGT ultima un cambio clave para el carnet de conducir que empieza en la autoescuela
articles.standfirst: Hasta hoy, si te sacas el carnet con un coche automático no puedes conducir manuales... pero eso va a cambiar
articles.summary: Hasta hoy, si te sacas el carnet con un coche automático no puedes conducir manuales... pero eso va a cambiar
articles.body: Actualmente hay dos modalidades para el obtener el permiso de conducción B para turismos: la convencional, mediante un vehículo con transmisión manual o una alternativa, si realizas las prácticas y el examen con un modelo con cambio automático, sin pedal de embrague. En el segundo de los casos, a los poseedores del permiso B se les incluye el llamado Código 78 que indica a las autoridades que no pueden manejar vehículos, digamos, 'convencionales'. Sin embargo, la realidad del mundo del automóvil está haciendo que, precisamente, lo 'convencional' ahora sean los coches con caja de cambios automáitca, sobre todo según va avanzando la electrificación. Los coches híbridos, híbridos enchufables y eléctricos tienen este tipo de transmisión en la que un mecanismo, en función de la situación de conducción y de los datos de los sensores del motor y de los sistemas electrónicos, ejecuta los cambios de marcha en función de la eficiencia y, en ocasiones, de la tracción. Hoy por hoy, las autoescuelas siguen recibiendo una inmensa mayoría de peticiones para obtener el carnet B con coches con cambio manual (un 95 por ciento) -tal como reconoce la DGT en su último número de la Revista Tráfico-, pero eso va a cambiar a corto plazo. Porque Tráfico ya trabaja con un cambio de normativa en el que el Cógido 78 desaparezca y, en su lugar, haya un camino diferente para que los que obtengan el carnet con un coche automático puedan conducir también los manuales. Y eso puede cambiarlo todo. La DGT establecerá como requisito un curso adicional, que en principio consistirá en un mínimo de siete horas de prácticas con coches manuales, para que exista la convalidación de ese Código 78.  La adopción de esta medida, además de para adecuar al conductor a la realidad de la industria automotriz (en la que los cambios manuales), se aplica para fomentar los vehículos electrificados. Incluso desde la Confederación Nacional de Autoescuelas (CNAE) se aplaude la iniciativa ya que se considera que con el cambio "el automático se convertirá en la principal puerta de entrada principal a la conducción". Desde tráfico y las autoescuelas se considera, además, que los coches automáticos tienen grandes ventajas ya que centra la atención del conductor en la carretera. Igualmente, los coches automáticos son más precisos y rápidos en los cambios de marchas y conllevan ventajas ecológicas (consumen y contaminan menos al gestionar la transmisión de forma más eficiente).

articles.title: AI-powered hackers: The new cyberwar is faster, smarter & harder to stop
articles.summary: News News: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a tool for cyberattacks, helping hackers automate tasks, move faster and coordinate complex operation.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a tool for cyberattacks, helping hackers automate tasks, move faster and coordinate complex operations.The result is a growing concern among cybersecurity experts: Has AI made it significantly easier to breach web systems?One of the most prominent recent examples emerged in July, when Taiwan's government agencies faced what officials described as a massive and unprecedented cyberattack. Taiwan's ministry of digital affairs said its monitoring systems detected the intrusion, triggering warnings and an investigation.Officials concluded that the attackers had combined conventional manual hacking with AI agents, including one reportedly called OpenClaw.According to Israeli cybersecurity firm Dream, the operation compromised nearly 21 government systems, breached 85 user accounts and extracted about 2,500 personnel records. The targets reportedly included Taiwan's justice ministry, nuclear safety agency and several energy companies."Thereâs still a human in there somewhere," Cris Thomas, a security researcher at Semgrep, told Reuters. "Somebody had to choose who to attack, had to establish an objective and give it a directive. Itâs not totally 100% autonomous. There was a capable operator in charge that did that."Taiwan, however, was not an isolated case.On November 13, 2025, Anthropic disclosed what it described as the first documented large-scale cyberattack carried out mostly without direct human involvement. The company said a state-linked group manipulated its Claude Code tool into attacking roughly 30 organisations worldwide, including financial institutions.The attackers reportedly broke the operation into small tasks and presented themselves as a legitimate cybersecurity firm conducting defensive tests. Anthropic estimated that AI performed 80% to 90% of the campaign, with humans intervening at only four to six critical decision points. At its peak, the system generated multiple requests every second, operating at a scale no human team could match.The significance of both cases lies not in AI independently "hacking the internet", but in its ability to connect and automate different stages of an attack: reconnaissance, credential theft, vulnerability discovery and movement through a network. All while a human sets the broader objective.How AI is lowering the barrier to cyberattacksAI has not reinvented cybercrime. What it has done is reduce the expertise, time and repetitive effort required to carry out many existing attack techniques.Prof Amgoth Tarachand of the Indian Institute of Technology (ISM) Dhanbad told TOI that AI can reduce the knowledge and labour traditionally required at different stages of an attack, without eliminating the need for human judgement or an actual path into the target.At its simplest, AI acts as an assistant: explaining unfamiliar code, drafting phishing messages or answering technical questions that would otherwise require hours of research.As an automation layer, it can handle repetitive work such as scanning, generating scripts and sorting data at speeds far beyond a human operator. As an agent, it can chain several tasks together towards an objective set by a human, checking back only when necessary.But that does not make cyberattacks fully autonomous."Cyberattacks are not simply programming problems," Amgoth said. "Successful operations require judgment: choosing targets, understanding unusual system behaviour, distinguishing genuine vulnerabilities from false positives, maintaining access, avoiding detection, and knowing what to do when circumstances change."AI can still make mistakes, misunderstand systems and confidently produce incorrect answers.A separate line of evidence points to the same shift. A report published this year by India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) describes attackers moving from manual, specialist operations towards repeatable, automated attack pipelines. Reconnaissance, exploit chaining and payload delivery are increasingly being industrialised "more like software manufacturing than tradecraft".The report also notes that AI removes human bandwidth as a constraint, allowing attackers to run multiple operations simultaneously without the fatigue and time limitations faced by human teams.Anthropic's own research illustrates the trend. The company reviewed 832 accounts linked to malicious activity between March 2025 and March 2026 and found AI being used across all 14 broad attack tactics in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, the industry's standard map of adversarial techniques. Anthropic said the proportion of those accounts rated medium-risk or higher increased from 33% to 56% during the period.On April 7, 2026, Anthropic also said its Claude Mythos Preview model had identified more than 23,000 potential software vulnerabilities during internal testing, including more than 1,000 rated high or critical severity. The company described the result as a "structural shift" from the capabilities of earlier models.These are Anthropic's own findings rather than independent measurements of what routinely happens across the internet. But they indicate that the technical ceiling of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery is rising rapidly.For Amgoth, the bigger change may be who can conduct a sophisticated operation."The long-term threat may not be 'AI teaches more people to hack,'" he said. "It may instead be one moderately skilled operator supervising what previously required a team of specialists."The shift is already visible in social engineering. Microsoft has reported an increase in the scale and sophistication of AI-assisted phishing, while Google has documented attackers using generative AI to create convincing, multilingual phishing messages, eliminating grammatical mistakes that once helped users identify scams."AI is converting expertise into a service and time into computation," Amgoth said. "Knowledge that previously took years to accumulate can increasingly be accessed on demand, and work that took hours can sometimes be compressed into minutes."That is what lowering the barrier really means. AI does not magically turn an inexperienced person into an elite hacker. It can, however, remove much of the slow, repetitive work that separates a moderately skilled operator from a much more capable team.Also read | Asked to solve a lab test, AI hacked the internet instead: When agents start doing things nobody told them to doCan anyone with AI hack into a web system?No.Having a web address and access to an AI chatbot does not mean someone can simply break into the system behind it. A URL tells an attacker where the door is. It does not give them the key.Given only a link, AI can help analyse a website from the outside, identifying technologies, explaining technical terminology and highlighting known weaknesses in software components it can detect. Google reported in May 2026 that threat actors were increasingly using AI to accelerate this kind of early-stage research."The URL tells the attacker where the door is. AI may help them examine the door far more intelligently, but there still has to be a weakness in the lock, a stolen key, or somebody willing to open it," Amgoth said.Google has also described a separate case involving a threat actor that used a zero-day exploit, a previously unknown software vulnerability, that the company believed had been developed with AI assistance.The frontier is clearly moving. But that does not mean every website is suddenly vulnerable because powerful AI exists. Real-world systems still rely on authentication, access controls, monitoring, rate limits, network segmentation and security patches. AI, meanwhile, remains capable of making basic mistakes.The critical change is therefore not that AI has removed the technical barriers to hacking. It has lowered some of the barriers surrounding them.AI for cyberdefenceThe same capabilities that make AI useful to attackers can give defenders a powerful advantage.Amgoth describes AI in cybersecurity as a force multiplier rather than a replacement for human defenders. The crucial advantage for defenders is access to information that an outside attacker normally does not have."While an attacker normally has only fragments of information about a web system, the defender can give AI visibility across the source code, software dependencies, identities, network activity, cloud infrastructure, application logs and organisational threat intelligence simultaneously," he said.That broader visibility can make AI particularly useful for finding vulnerabilities, detecting unusual behaviour and identifying attack patterns.In February 2026, Anthropic reported that its models could identify previously unknown, high-severity vulnerabilities in mature, well-tested codebases and described a system that could scan repositories and suggest patches for human review.Google's Mandiant division reported in August 2026 that it had developed a similar agentic approach to source-code review, using it in penetration testing and incident response.AI-assisted monitoring can also process enormous volumes of security data much faster than human analysts working through logs manually. CERT-In's report, particularly in the context of the financial sector, describes a shift from periodic security checks towards continuous monitoring because attackers operating at machine speed cannot be reliably countered by reviews conducted once a quarter.But AI-driven defence comes with its own risks. Giving an AI system broad access to source code, cloud infrastructure or credentials creates a new potential point of failure if the system is poorly controlled. Google's Mandiant team has also warned about the risks associated with deploying privileged AI agents without appropriate safeguards.The balance, therefore, is not simply between hackers and AI.It is between AI-assisted attackers and AI-assisted defenders.The Taiwan attack and Anthropic's disclosure demonstrate how AI can allow attackers to accomplish more with fewer people and less time. Faster code analysis, faster reconnaissance and faster iteration can turn what once required a team of specialists into a much more automated operation.But those same capabilities are available to defenders, and defenders typically have access to far more information about their own systems than an attacker can obtain from the outside.The barrier is falling on both sides.The question is no longer whether AI will make cyberattacks easier. It already has for many stages of an operation. The bigger question is who will use AI more effectively, the attacker trying to exploit a weakness or the defender trying to plug it?

articles.title: Trump plans to grow his way out of $40 trillion debt crisis—it’s a ‘fantastic story’ but virtually impossible, says top budget economist
articles.summary: "If you tell the debt markets: 'Hey, we think we're gonna be able to grow our way out of this,' and then a year later they're not seeing any improvements fro...
articles.body:
The U.S. national debt has hit $40 trillion , and the Trump administration is facing questions about its budget plans as a result. The good news is, there has one: The American economy will apparently grow its way out of any fiscal crisis. "It's been a problem for 35 years," Trump told reporters Friday. "And what we have now … is we have tremendous growth. And the way you take care of debt is with growth, and we have tremendous growth. We've never had growth like we have right now." "There's nothing magic about the $40 trillion number," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC last week, "And we can grow our way out of that."

Economists would be inclined to agree with Bessent: The value of the debt, while an extraordinary milestone, doesn't hold much relative weight. What economists (and more importantly, the bond market) is watching is the debt-to-GDP ratio: This demonstrates the level of borrowing by a country against its economic capacity to repay and service it.

Currently, the U.S. ratio stands at 122%. To bring it back into a lower balance, an economy could cut its borrowing or—as Bessent suggests—increase its growth.

When the alternative is cutting borrowing and, as a result, government spending, the growth plan is a more optimistic and politically palatable route.

It's also the latest in a series of solutions proposed by the White House: Originally, President Trump had suggested that tariffs would pay down the national debt (the plan was quickly nixed by a Supreme Court ruling ordering the administration to repay approximately $100 billion in revenues that the justices deemed illegal).

Trump later suggested a "golden visa" strategy —selling rich immigrants visas at $5 million each—could pay down the national debt. The policies were novel, but economists broadly welcomed action by the Trump Administration on the fiscal picture.

But now there a bond market reckoning looming. The risk premium demanded by investors for holding the 30-year Treasury rose to over 5.3% in recent days, prompting U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to deploy $4 billion or more in unscheduled buybacks. If the U.S. can't pay its debt, the worst-case scenario is a default crisis.

So, can the U.S. grow its way out of debt? It's a "fantastic story," says Kent Smetters , Boettner Professor of economics and public policy at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania.

Unfortunately, Professor Smetters—the faculty director of a fiscal analysis tool called the Penn Wharton Budget Model—says the plan is also "pretty clearly" not feasible. He explained in an interview with Fortune : "People often get the causality kind of opposite. They think more growth, less of a debt problem, and in reality, it's just the opposite … We deal with the debt issue in order to try to aid economic growth, not vice versa."

Robert Kiyosaki has never been shy about issuing dire financial warnings. But with America's national debt reaching a staggering new milestone, the Rich Dad Poor Dad author is turning up the volume.

"$40 TRILLION US NATIONAL [debt] soon!!" Kiyosaki wrote (1) on X. "What are you doing about it?"

The warning proved timely. America's national debt has now crossed the $40 trillion threshold, according to data from the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Debt to the Penny (2) database.

Kiyosaki believes the country's growing debt burden will ultimately punish people who depend heavily on cash.

"Remember: Savers of cash are the BIGGEST LOSERS!!!!" he declared.

Days later, Kiyosaki doubled down after the Treasury (3) announced it would at least double the size of certain buyback operations involving longer-dated government debt, raising them from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation.

"PRINTING MORE FAKE $," Kiyosaki wrote (4), characterizing the Treasury's move as "another round of quantitative easing."

He argued that the policy would weaken the U.S. Dollar Index and cause inflation to accelerate — leaving "savers of fake $" as "the biggest losers."

However, it's important to distinguish Kiyosaki's characterization from what the Treasury actually announced. These are liquidity-support buybacks intended to improve trading conditions in portions of the Treasury market. They're not technically the same as quantitative easing, which is conducted by the Federal Reserve and expands the Fed's balance sheet.

Still, Kiyosaki's broader concern is easy to understand, especially given how steadily inflation has eroded the dollar's purchasing power over time.

According to the Inflation Calculator (5) on the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis website, $100 in 2026 has the same purchasing power as just $11.74 did in 1970.

That's right. $100 became less than $12.

"Educated investors who invest in assets that go up in value, such as gold, silver, Bitcoin, some real estate, get richer… while people who are financially uneducated and invest in fake assets get poorer," he wrote.

articles.title: The Movement: MAHA and anti-abortion groups split on FDA nominee
articles.summary: Anti-abortion groups and other conservatives largely applauded the White House announcement that President Trump would nominate health policy aide Dr. Heidi Overton for Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner, viewing her as their champion for, among other things, bringing an end to medication abortion. But others in the conservative world were less thrilled. Overton is not…
articles.body:
Anti-abortion groups and other conservatives largely applauded the White House announcement that President Trump would nominate health policy aide Dr. Heidi Overton for Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner, viewing her as their champion for, among other things, bringing an end to medication abortion.

But others in the conservative world were less thrilled. Overton is not a favorite of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, whose proponents see her as an obstacle to their goals.

Alex Clark , a MAHA podcaster, told her followers to press their senators against confirming Overton, citing her involvement in an executive order earlier this year that boosted production of glyphosate herbicides, something the MAHA movement is staunchly against.

Clark, in a series of posts on social platform X, said Overton “wrote” the executive order and “has EXTENSIVE personal ties to Bayer,” referring to the pharmaceutical and biotech giant that produces many herbicides.

“Everyone knows she is the biggest roadblock in the admin when it comes to getting several true MAHA initiatives done,” Clark said of Overton. Several unnamed sources said the same in a story about Overton in The Atlantic last month.

Clark’s fervor provoked a White House spokesperson, Kush Desai , to push back online.

“Anyone suggesting that Heidi wrote this EO [executive order], has ties to Bayer, or isn’t MAHA has no clue what they’re talking about,” Desai said. “Pretty much every MAHA win by this Administration absolutely would not have been possible without Heidi often singlehandedly running interagency policy processes.”

Clark dug further in, saying “MAHA moms are smarter than this” and arguing that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is “the most capable fighter we have” but that he’s surrounded by people who “share none of his values.”

The divisions over Overton show an area of friction between the MAHA and the anti-abortion wings of Trump’s coalition. That’s significant as Republicans and the White House look to shore up their base in advance of the midterms and 2028 because both groups are passionate sectors of Trump’s support and risking either is dangerous for Republicans going forward.

Anti-abortion conservatives, for the most part, have been rooting for the administration’s agenda since the beginning, although some have expressed disappointment at what they see as a lack of progress. They’re pushing Trump to crack down further on mifepristone and permanently strip federal funding from Planned Parenthood.

Overton’s appointment is a signal to those anti-abortion advocates that the administration is still moving toward those goals. Overton has denounced abortion and called for more restrictions on prescribing mifepristone. That’s especially relevant as the FDA is currently reviewing the safety of the drug.

Anti-abortion groups lauded Overton’s promotion last week.

“She has the scientific and medical background that will enable her to perform an objective analysis of the dangers chemical abortion poses to women,” John Mize , CEO of Americans United for Life, said in a statement .

Lila Rose , president of Live Action, congratulated Overton in a post on X .

“This is a chance to restore trust and put health over politics,” Rose said. “Dr. Overton should pull the deadly abortion pill from the market. Step one: end mail-order abortions that kill babies even in pro-life states.”

There were other Republican voices against Overton for different reasons. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate committee that will process Overton’s nomination, said he had “strong concerns” about her stance on childhood vaccine recommendations, which has been a sticking point between Cassidy, also a medical doctor, and the administration.

Overton stood next to Trump at a recent ceremony where he signed an executive order paring down the childhood vaccine recommendations. In that, she is aligned with the MAHA movement and Kennedy.

Conservative commentator Laura Loomer also spoke out against Overton, alleging Overton was involved in Health and Human Services’s (HHS) “MAHA Report,” which came out last May and was soon discovered to contain thousands of fake citations .

“Now that Heidi Overton has been selected as the head of the FDA, I’ll remind everyone that she was one of the officials involved in the publication of the notorious and highly embarrassing White House ‘MAHA report’, which was full of fake and AI citations,” Loomer said in a post .

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

The next step in the Republican midterm strategy: hype.

Republicans will be looking to harness pep rally-style hype, viral moments and strong party unity at the Republican National Committee (RNC) convention in Dallas in a few weeks. The event is the first of its kind: in a normal cycle, national party conventions like this are held every four years as a chance to crown a presidential nominee.

But this is not a normal cycle. Republicans are seeing polls that point against them in races down the ballot and around the country as Trump’s approval ratings remain low. In primary elections all over, Democratic voters have turned out in swarms while many Republicans have stayed home.

Republicans are hoping to course-correct with a rousing rally in a key Senate battleground. A GOP strategist told me that the goal is to “build enthusiasm” for the election and remind voters of the stakes if Republicans lose their majorities in Congress, pitching it as “common-sense versus communism.”

Neil Newhouse , Republican strategist and partner at Public Opinion Strategies, told me by email that news of the convention doesn’t seem to have broken through to voters much yet. There are few details about what will happen there besides a website with a list of potential speakers that includes Trump, most of his Cabinet, and a handful of governors, members of Congress, and other prominent MAGA World names.

But if the convention can create some steam to power the Republican message into November, Newhouse said it could be useful.

“To the extent that this convention can reach some of these disaffected or disinterested GOP faithful and reinforce what’s at stake in this election, that could make a significant difference on election day,” Newhouse said.

The stated goals of the convention, according to the website, are as follows: celebrating “the America First agenda” as Trump has enacted it thus far in his term; christening “the American comeback” by “recognizing hardworking Americans … whose work is driving economic growth, advancing energy dominance, and ushering in a new Golden Age of American prosperity”; and celebrating the 250th anniversary of the United States.

Douglas Heye , a former RNC chair and Republican strategist, told me he’s looking to hear more about the agenda for the convention. Although novel, he said, he sees the appeal of the event.

“The idea isn’t a bad one — that it’s not been done before is not a concern, trying something different given historical midterm trends could be helpful, especially for fundraising,” Heye said.

It’s no coincidence that this will all go down at the American Airlines Center in Dallas. Texas’s Senate race between state Attorney General Ken Paxton , who has Trump’s endorsement, and state legislator James Talarico is one of the most expensive and closely watched Senate contests in history.

The timing is also strategic. The two-day event will run Sept. 9-10, right as primaries end and before early voting for November’s general election begins.

“I’ve advised President Trump against this course of action for a year because American ranchers have been struggling against the packer monopoly for decades, and this will further harm them – most of whom are MAGA Republicans,” Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) said on X .

The Republican runoff for the Oklahoma governor’s mansion will be, in some ways, a test of how powerful Trump’s endorsement is for Oklahoma primary voters, especially against a high-profile state official like Drummond. articles.title: French has become a sticking point in the Canada-US trade dispute. Here’s why
articles.summary: As a trade war between the United States and Canada looms following the collapse of talks last week, a key issue has emerged: French language laws.
articles.body:
As a trade war between the United States and Canada looms following the collapse of talks last week, a key issue has emerged that's further inflamed tensions between the longtime allies: French language laws.

Canada is a bilingual country and has laws protecting both of its official languages: English and French, the first language spoken for roughly one fifth of the population, including nearly 85% of primarily Francophone province of Quebec.

Among the laws, product labels must be displayed in both English and French, and US streaming platforms must support and promote Canadian content (including Indigenous and French Canadian content) to audiences north of the border.

Canada's language requirements have long been viewed by the US as a trade barrier but are generally a red line for Ottawa — which Prime Minister Mark Carney enforced by walking away from a deal which he said included "threats to French language and culture."

On Monday, Carney said Canada "could not accept" the proposed deal that would have weakened French language protections, telling reporters that his government "will not give (the US) what they have asked."

Many in Canada have rallied behind Carney's decision — and particularly his comments about protecting French culture, a core part of Canada's national identity.

After US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called Ottawa's concerns about French a "funny, fake story" on Monday, the Canadian leader denied the issue was a laughing matter, saying there is an "enormous gap between our perspective and the US perspective."

"For Americans, French language, Francophone culture, Canadian culture, these are irritants," Carney said in French at a news conference in Lévis, Quebec.

"Here in Quebec, here in Canada, these are rights," he said, as a group of reporters applauded.

On Tuesday, President Donald Trump denied that the US wanted to interfere with Canada's French language laws and accused Carney of using the issue to score political points in Quebec in a post to Truth Social.

"I would never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing. This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec," the US president posted.

His post came the same day Canada announced tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on over 700 American goods, including reciprocal 50% duties on US steel and aluminum, set to take effect September 8.

articles.title: WhatsApp tightens account security with stronger two-step verification and more | TechCrunch
articles.summary: WhatsApp’s two-step verification previously relied on a six-digit PIN, but now users can choose a longer, alphanumeric password with special characters.
articles.body:
WhatsApp announced Tuesday that it’s launching new security features and updates to help users keep their accounts secure, including stronger two-step verification and the ability to add more than one passkey to your account. The Meta-owned app is also adding context to calls from unknown numbers.

The updates come as WhatsApp and other messaging apps, such as Signal and Telegram , look to make account security easier and more accessible for everyday users, especially as phishing and hacking attempts have become more sophisticated over the years.

Until now, WhatsApp’s two-step verification has used a six-digit PIN as an extra layer of protection to prevent someone from taking over an account even if they’re able to obtain the user’s one-time passcode. Now, users can choose a longer, alphanumeric password with special characters to make the PIN harder to guess.

As for passkeys, users can now add more than one passkey to their account, which WhatsApps says will be useful if a person uses both iOS and Android.

Passkeys, which WhatsApp launched support for in 2024 , are far stronger than passwords and allow users to log in to their accounts using Face ID or their fingerprint. Passkeys remove the need to rely on username and password combinations, which are ordinarily susceptible to phishing attacks. Passkey logins make it harder for bad actors to remotely access your accounts, as an attacker would need physical access to a person’s device that stores the user’s part of the passkey.

Additionally, Android users will now see more information when they’re getting a call from someone who isn’t in their contacts, like whether the number is from a different country and if they have any groups in common with the caller.

The latest features join the growing list of updates WhatsApp has rolled out in recent months. The company launched usernames in late June to allow people to share their profiles without disclosing their phone number. In late May, Meta launched a subscription plan for the messaging app that unlocks extra features, like profile customization, super reactions, story insights, and more.

The WhatsApp Plus plan launched alongside similar “Plus” offerings for Instagram and Facebook.

President Donald Trump is looking to overhaul the federal homelessness policy, moving away from housing subsidies and toward mandatory treatment for people struggling with mental illness or substance abuse. The administration is also pursuing policies that would make sleeping or camping on public streets illegal.

A team from Cicero Institute , a think tank founded by billionaire and Trump ally Joe Lonsdale, has traveled across the country pushing lawmakers to criminalize public camping and sleeping on streets.

According to the New York Times, 21 states have considered camping bans or other homelessness laws backed by Cicero, with 16 ultimately passing them. The group is now working with the Trump administration to redirect federal funding away from housing subsidies and toward forced treatment programs.

Homelessness has neared record highs. In January 2025 , when Trump took office for his second term, nearly 746,000 people were experiencing homelessness. The increase has led some Republicans to embrace tougher measures to clear streets and, according to the New York Times, no group has pushed harder than Cicero Institute.

The group's central target is Housing First , the current federal policy on homelessness. The measure prioritizes getting people into stable housing before addressing issues such as addiction or mental health. The policy was embraced by Trump during his first term. The administration now argues the policy ignores the root cause of homelessness by providing housing subsidies but making treatment optional — a sentiment backed by Cicero.

Critics, however, argue that housing is itself a crucial first step in helping people stabilize their lives and that there is limited evidence that forcing people into treatment will reduce homelessness.

In July 2025, the administration issued an executive order called "Ending Crime and Disorder on American Streets," which includes a camping ban.

articles.title: Callaway apologizes for ‘Good Good’ ad showing woman shoved to ground

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Callaway CEO Chip Brewer said the video, which was posted over the weekend on Good Good Golf social channels,…
articles.body:
Golf company Callaway is apologizing for an advertisement for a new driver posted by its media partner Good Good Golf that depicted violence against women and was subsequently taken down.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Callaway CEO Chip Brewer said the video, which was posted over the weekend on Good Good Golf social channels, was approved by Callaway and said it should not have been.

“Mistakes were made,” Brewer said, adding the company is still investigating how the advertisement, which he said does not reflect the company’s values, was approved.

The ad in question was promoting a new Good Good Golf quantum driver Callaway is rolling out this week.

It shows a woman, a member of the Good Good Golf content team, reaching for the driver when the company’s co-founder, Garrett Clark, rushes after her and knocks her to the ground.

“Don’t touch my driver,” Clark angrily says in the video while standing over her.

Following widespread backlash online, Good Good Golf took the video down and apologized for its content.

“Good Good has always stood for making the game more inclusive for all and we will continue to ensure that is our mission moving forward,” the company said.

Callaway did not say if it was reviewing its partnership with Good Good Golf but insisted “it will learn from this and do better.”

articles.title: Biden Added $8 Trillion To The National Debt Making Him The 3rd Biggest Spending President. You Can Probably Guess Who Is #1
articles.summary: With federal debt crossing $40 trillion, analysts are ranking presidents by how much they borrowed, and the results challenge some popular assumptions about...
articles.body:
Trump leads recent presidents with $12 trillion in combined debt added, followed by Obama at $9 trillion and Biden at $8 trillion.

Biden's single term added more debt than Trump's entire first term, placing him third only because Trump's two terms are combined.

Mandatory spending and interest payments now consume over 60% of the federal budget, with interest costs alone exceeding Pentagon funding.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now .

Federal debt outstanding crossed $40 trillion on or around Aug. 19, 2026. That doubling has revived ranking presidents by debt added. Using Treasury's "Debt to the Penny" series from start to end of term in nominal dollars, Joe Biden's single term added roughly $8.45 trillion, placing him third among the last five presidents. Donald Trump ranks first; Barack Obama second.

Measured by actual increase in total public debt outstanding: Trump, both terms combined, roughly $11.63 trillion, of which roughly $7.80 trillion came in term one and roughly $3.83 trillion in the first 19 months of term two; Obama, two terms, roughly $9.32 trillion; Biden, one term, roughly $8.45 trillion; George W. Bush, two terms, roughly $4.90 trillion; and Reagan, two terms, roughly $1.86 trillion.

Trump ranks first because his two non-consecutive terms are combined. Measured term by term, Biden's roughly $8.45 trillion exceeds Trump's first term of roughly $7.80 trillion. His second term is still in progress, so his total will keep growing and is not a finished, comparable number like the others. Combining terms is a legitimate approach and the one Newsweek used in its Aug. 20, 2026 analysis, which independently produced essentially the same totals.

The "$8 trillion" is rounded shorthand for the roughly $8.45 trillion Treasury figure. A debt increase reflects the gap between spending and revenue plus other financing needs, not spending alone. Tax cuts, revenue shortfalls, and interest costs each contribute independently. "Spending president" is common shorthand; the label is imprecise.

A separate measurement matters. The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, in an April 3, 2025 analysis, estimated that Biden-era legislation and executive actions added a projected $4.7 trillion in new debt over a 10-year window, scored at enactment. That figure differs from Treasury's $8.45 trillion. CRFB counts only new policy choices as scored at enactment; it excludes pre-existing mandatory spending growth, revenue performance, and rising interest costs on existing debt. The two figures are not in conflict.

Billionaire Ray Dalio warned last week that the U.S. is heading for a major debt crisis, likening the nation to a person on the verge of a heart attack.

articles.title: 2 measles-related deaths reported in Pennsylvania
articles.summary: Two Pennsylvanians have died after contracting measles, the state’s health department said Tuesday. Both people, who were unvaccinated, lived in Lancaster County. The state health department said in a release it will not identify the deceased to protect their privacy and that of their families. Their deaths marked the first measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania in…
articles.body:
Two Pennsylvanians have died after contracting measles, the state’s health department said Tuesday.

Both people, who were unvaccinated, lived in Lancaster County. The state health department said in a release it will not identify the deceased to protect their privacy and that of their families.

Their deaths marked the first measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania in 35 years and the first in the country this year.

The U.S. has now seen five measles deaths in the last two years, more than the combined total of reported deaths over the past three decades.

During a press conference Tuesday, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) blamed misinformation for declining vaccination rates — specifically calling out the Trump administration.

“When the information we see coming from the federal government, in some cases, isn’t driven by facts and by science, it makes it even more confusing for parents, and that has a serious impact,” Shapiro said.

Shapiro, widely seen as a Democratic presidential contender in 2028, added that he spoke with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. by phone on Tuesday about the two deaths.

“I was very, very blunt with him, and I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said.

“There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors and actual medical professionals to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids,” he continued.

Shapiro said he declined Kennedy’s offer of federal staffers to help with the outbreak.

Debra Bogen, the state’s health secretary, said her “deepest sympathies” are with the loved ones of the two deceased Pennsylvanians.

“Because measles was largely eliminated in the Commonwealth for more than three decades, people are not familiar with this disease and don’t fully understand the potential severity of the illness,” Bogen said in a release. “We want to ensure every Pennsylvanian has the information they need to protect themselves, their loved ones and their communities.”

The state health department noted it has confirmed 393 cases in 28 counties so far this year. Public health officials have confirmed 2,777 cases in the U.S. as of Thursday, with 94 percent of those cases associated with 36 outbreaks, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In a statement co-signed by the CDC and its governing body, the Health and Human Services Department, the agency wrote that it is “working closely with state and local health departments to strengthen response efforts, rapidly support affected communities across the state, and communicate the steps people can take to slow the spread of measles.”

“The MMR vaccine provides the most effective protection against measles and helps prevent its spread. CDC will continue to follow Pennsylvania’s lead and provide resources to support the state’s response,” the statement continued.

Bogen noted the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “safe and provides the best protection we have against measles.”

Earlier this month, President Trump signed an executive order that proposes splitting up the MMR vaccine for children. The combined shot has been available since 1971, and doctors recommend kids receive it twice: at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years.

On the day he signed the order, Trump said the MMR vaccine was “lethal” in some cases, contradicting established medical consensus.

“Together there could be a possibility they are quite lethal,” the president said in the Oval Office. “And separately it looks like they are not at all lethal but just very effective.”

The heads of multiple medical groups, including the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics , have pushed back on Trump’s order — which also called for reducing the number of core vaccinations every child should receive to 11. Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, also noted on Sunday that the MMR vaccine is not lethal.

This story was updated at 4:42 p.m. on Aug. 25, 2026.

articles.title: Apple rescues Hide My Email feature from the privacy scrap heap
articles.summary: Apple says it will no longer ditch using its icloud.com domain for hiding people's email addresses.
articles.body:
Apple has reneged on a planned change to its Hide My Email feature that users said would have made the privacy tool less effective.

Hide My Email is a privacy feature for paying iCloud+ users that generates a unique and disposable email address to give websites instead of a person’s real email address and still have emails route to their regular inboxes. The benefit of the email-hiding feature is that privately generated email addresses cannot be distinguished from regular Apple users with an @icloud.com email address. However, the feature still allows Apple to tell law enforcement who is behind a masked email address .

Earlier this year, the company said it would move users to @private.icloud.com , which users said would make it easier for websites to reject these email addresses during sign-ups. On social media and Reddit threads, users criticized the change as defeating the purpose of the service altogether.

The company confirmed an update on Monday that Hide My Email addresses “will remain” on @icloud.com , after previously saying it would move users to @private.icloud.com .

Apple did not give a reason for changing its decision, but Daring Fireball’s John Gruber , who first reported the about-face, said that Apple employees had objected to the change all along.

Earlier this year, 404 Media reported that a bug in Hide My Email revealed people’s real email addresses. Apple fixed the bug more than a year after it was first made aware that emails rejected as spam would leak the masked users’ real email addresses.

articles.title: JPMorgan compares Bessent's $4B bond buyback to 'paying your mortgage with your credit card' as U.S. debt hits $40T
articles.summary: The bond market is a mess, but what do all the recent developments mean?
articles.body:
Debt by any other name is still debt, and if you've ever been in any amount of it, you'll know that the one thing that is definitely not the solution is, well, even more debt. And yet, that seems to be the preferred strategy of modern governments: If more money is needed, then they can simply fund it with endless debt.

The level of arrears accrued by the powers of the world is almost incomprehensible at this point. According to the Institute of International Finance, total global debt , across sectors and types of lending, is over $350 trillion, equivalent to about 305% of global GDP. That's compared to 240% of GDP in 2005.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Our comfort with using borrowed money is why, perhaps, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is so confident in his latest scheme to curb concerns over waning demand for bonds — buying back more of the debt to simply reissue it under different terms.

The plan, outlined late last week , is intended to improve market conditions by soaking up longer-term bonds with high yield rates as people become increasingly wary of how the investment vehicles will perform in these economically uncertain times.

The problem with the buyback is the fact that the Treasury will issue shorter-term bonds to pay for it, which, according to JPMorgan's James Sullivan, is akin to "paying your mortgage with your credit card" as it "can work for a while, but eventually the mismatch starts to become more obvious."

Sullivan, who serves as the firm's co-head of global fundamental research, made the comparison on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Aug. 21 , warning that the Treasury is only deferring the problem of the glaring debt to a later date. Though the department is unfortunately quite limited in how it can deal with the situation in any meaningful capacity, experts remain critical of the temporary fix.

Instant effects — but what about long-term?

The announcement had the effect of immediately pushing 30-year treasury yields — which had reached a ceiling of 5.34% last week, the highest seen in 19 years — to 5.18% , though they have since risen back to close to 5.25% .

Some argue that the unexpected timing of the action was the action, including Padhraic Garvey, ING bank's Head of American Research, who admits that though the recovery will merely "dampen but not abort the pressure."

articles.title: That fake Grand Theft Auto VI demo is actually just malware | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Grand Theft Auto fans, eager for news about one of the most anticipated video games of all time, appear especially vulnerable to this new cyberattack.
articles.body:
In the long wait for the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI, an open-world game about crime, some in the gaming community are being targeted by cybercriminals in the real world.

Fans are still waiting for the game more than a decade after the release of GTA 5, which sold more copies than any game ever, except for Minecraft. Now, after multiple GTA 6 delays and with some fans desperate for any scrap of news, hackers are using the cover as a perfect opportunity to target eager gamers.

Cybercriminals have created fake websites impersonating Rockstar, the developer behind GTA 6. These websites advertise a playable GTA 6 demo — but no legitimate demo exists. Once the unsuspecting gamer clicks the “Play Now” button, they download a file that looks like a game installer, but is actually malware, according to the cybersecurity company Malwarebytes .

The malware is an information stealer that is designed to find and take a victim’s passwords, cookies, and logged-in sessions stored in their web browser. These attacks can in some cases allow hackers to log in as if they were the account holder, even when protected by multi-factor authentication.

After multiple delays, GTA 6 is expected to release on November 19, 2026. On Thursday, Netflix will air an extended look at the game, which could perhaps answer some questions about the legitimacy of various leaks.

A relevant reminder as always: Don’t download stuff if you aren’t sure it comes from a reliable source.

articles.title: Study suggests at least 25 percent of NFL players get CTE
articles.summary: A Tuesday report found that at least 25 percent of deceased NFL players who were studied suffered from chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in their lives. A team of researchers published a report in the British Medical Journal analyzing the brains of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021. Over the last six years…
articles.body:
A Tuesday report found that at least 25 percent of deceased NFL players who were studied suffered from chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in their lives.

A team of researchers published a report in the British Medical Journal analyzing the brains of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021.

Over the last six years of the study, researchers received 235 brains of the 878 NFL players who died. In that sample, 215 brains — 24.5 percent — were diagnosed with CTE. They estimated the prevalence of the disease could be far higher in those years as researchers were unable to analyze the other 643 brains that were not donated.

“The possible prevalence at death [of CTE] during 2016 to 2021, when brain donation was most frequent, ranged between 24.5 percent and 97.7 percent,” they wrote.

The study also noted that late-stage CTE is more prevalent in donors with dementia as research continues to trace the exact causes of the disease.

Another 2017 study in the Journal of American Medical Association reported similar results in the brains of 111 deceased NFL players; all but one were found to have CTE in the study.

The Mayo Clinic calls CTE a brain disease that can likely be caused by repeated head trauma and can cause emotional distress, mood swings and impact an individual’s behavior. The only way to be diagnosed with the disease is posthumously during a brain autopsy.

It outlined that CTE “appears to be related to repeated head injuries, often occurring in contact sports or military combat.”

The league most notably faced criticism when former Dallas Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland was diagnosed with the condition after dying by suicide in 2025.

Researchers at Boston University also found that former New England Patriots player Aaron Hernandez, who died by suicide at 27, had the worst case of CTE seen in a young person, with his brain resembling that of a 60 year old.

The NFL Players Association, in a statement to ESPN , said that the study was “a sobering reminder that football carries real risks, and those risks can have lasting consequences for players and their families.”

“The findings should serve as a call to action across the entire football ecosystem. We all share a responsibility to advance research, improve access to care, develop better treatments, and support those affected by the long-term impacts of the game,” the association continued.

According to the British Medical Journal, 1,712 former NFL players died between 2008 and 2021, with 338 brains donated for research.

articles.title: Thyroid tablets recalled nationwide over potential ‘superpotency’: FDA
articles.summary: Patients taking the affected lot are advised not to discontinue use without first consulting their health care provider.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Vitruvias Therapeutics is voluntarily recalling one lot of thyroid tablet s because they could potentially be “superpotent,” federal regulators announced this week.

The high potency 30mg tablets could cause hyperthyroidism, or an overactive thyroid, according to the Food and Drug Administration . The affected lot (504950) was distributed nationwide to Vitruvias Therapeutics’ direct accounts from Jan. 31 to Sept. 30, 2025.

Consuming the recalled tablets could result in “weight loss, heat intolerance, fatigue, nervousness, muscle weakness, hypertension, chest pain, rapid heart rate, or heart rhythm disturbances,” the FDA warned. The elderly, pregnant women and infants are at the greatest risk.

Of the 3,655 units released, only 1955 were sold, the agency added.

Vitruvias Therapeutics is currently notifying wholesalers to stop distributing the recalled product and to arrange for its destruction.

The company hasn’t received any reports of negative impacts from the recalled tablets, which are used to treat hypothyroidism, or an underactive thyroid, the FDA added. Patients taking the affected lot are advised not to discontinue use without first consulting their health care provider.

For questions, consumers can contact Vitruvias Therapeutics by email at safety@vitruvias.com or by phone at (256) 239-9373 during standard business hours.

articles.title: Polestar claims it was blindsided by sales ban
articles.summary: Polestar thought it would be approved to continue selling its EVs in the US, and was blindsided by the Trump administration’s rejection of its application.
articles.body: Polestar said the Trump administration strung it along for months before finally rejecting its request to continue selling its electric vehicles in the US under a rule outlawing vehicles with connected software from China. In an August 18th letter sent to dealers and obtained by The Verge, Polestar said it doesn’t have a clear answer as to why its application to continue selling its EVs in the US was denied, considering its sister company Volvo was authorized to sell its vehicles despite similar corporate ownership. (The letter was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.) The US Department of Commerce approved Volvo in May 2026 to continue importing and selling its vehicles in the US, despite restrictions tied to its majority Chinese owner, Geely. But one month later, the department rejected Polestar’s similar request, leading to the company to announce it would stop selling its vehicles in the US starting with the 2027 model year. The rule, which originated under the Biden administration, bans the import and sale of vehicles with connected software from hostile countries, including China. In the letter to dealers, Polestar’s head of product Peter Wexler lays out the timeline of the company’s communications with the Trump administration, starting with a May 29, 2025 application to the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) under the Commerce Department. In subsequent meetings, Wexler says Polestar was given the impression that Polestar would be approved, considering its vehicles are functionally similar to Volvo’s. Jeffrey Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, said during an in-person meeting with Polestar’s representatives “that it would be reasonable for Polestar to expect approval of its applications if Volvo Cars was approved to sell its cars under effectively the same shareholding and ownership structure and with the same hardware and software in the Polestar 3 as the Volvo EX90,” Wexler writes. Polestar told the administration it open to a variety of “mitigation measures” to ensure its vehicles were compliant with the ban on Chinese software, including regular audits, geographic restrictions on data storage and management, and limitations on digital keys and remote access. But the administration declined all such offers, Wexler said. “BIS never engaged in any such discussions with Polestar,” he writes. “Instead, BIS communicated that it had all the information it required to render a decision.” Wexler said that Polestar is continuing to press the administration for an explanation on why it was denied approval. The company was sued recently by Polestar dealer Prestige Imports in New Jersey, which accuses the company of engineering its own exit from the US by failing to do enough to satisfy regulators at the Commerce Department.

articles.title: 9/11 victim identified nearly 25 years later with new forensic technique
articles.summary: The terrorist attack killed 2,753 people in New York City.
articles.body:
NEW YORK ( WPIX ) — As the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks approaches, a victim has been identified, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday.

The adult woman was identified using a breakthrough technique of forensic investigative genetic genealogy, or FIGG.

She is the first 9/11 victim identified using the technique and the 1,654th victim identified through analysis of remains recovered from the attacks, according to officials. The terrorist attack killed 2,753 people in New York City.

“As we approach the 25th anniversary of the horrific Sept. 11 attacks, we honor the nearly 3,000 people whose lives were stolen that day, and we remain committed to the families who have spent 25 years waiting for answers,” Mamdani said.

“The identification of this victim through forensic investigative genetic genealogy is a powerful example of what is possible when we pair cutting-edge technology with an unwavering commitment to those we lost,” the mayor added.

FIGG pairs specialized DNA technologies with genealogical investigative techniques to produce leads in identifying victims. They are then confirmed through the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner through DNA and other forensic methods.

The name of the victim is being withheld at the request of the family.

Before Monday, the last time a victim of the 9/11 attacks at the World Trade Center was identified was in August 2025.

articles.title: What is CTE, and how many former NFL players have been diagnosed with it?
articles.summary: So far, the degenerative brain disease has only been diagnosed after a person’s death.
articles.body:
Editor’s Note: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org .

(NEXSTAR) – A new study led by researchers out of Massachusetts suggests that among those who have played in the NFL, at least one in four may develop chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a disease that carries no cure and has only been diagnosed after death.

The study , published in The BMJ, reviewed the hundreds of NFL players who died between 2008 and 2021. Of the more than 1,700 who died, researchers reported that the brains of 338 were studied. Postmortem brain analysis has, so far, been the only proven method of determining whether someone has CTE, a degenerative brain disease.

Of the 338 brains that were studied, it was determined that 315 donors had a CTE diagnosis.

Among players who died within the last six years – a time in which “brain donation was more frequent” – researchers said 235 NFL players donated their brains for analysis. More than 210 were found to have CTE.

Just over 200 of the 338 whose brains were analyzed had been previously diagnosed with dementia. The study found that donors with dementia were later found to have more severe cases of CTE: 94 had Stage 4 CTE, considered the most severe level.

Broadly speaking, CTE impacts how the brain functions. Research has suggested that CTE is “linked to a build-up of abnormal proteins that damage brain tissue and cause brain cells to undergo cell death,” the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention explains .

CTE is often found in people who have experienced repeated impacts to the head, making football players among the most commonly associated with the disease. However, as the Boston University CTE Center notes , the condition has been linked to boxers and soccer and hockey players, as well as those who have served in the military or as first responders. Even athletes who stopped participating in sports in high school and college have been diagnosed with CTE.

Symptoms can take years or decades to develop, experts say. When they do appear, they can last for months or years. The exact symptoms associated with CTE are unclear, but the CDC explains that those who are diagnosed are later described as having “problems with thinking, emotions, mood, suicidal thoughts and/or behaviors that became serious enough to get in the way of normal daily activities.”

“However, having these symptoms does not necessarily mean a person has CTE,” the CDC adds. “It is important to talk to a doctor if you, a family member, or friend have any questions or concerns. Treatments are available to help with many of these symptoms.”

Research to better understand CTE – including how it develops, what risk factors may be associated with it, and how to diagnose it earlier – continues, according to Boston University.

Hundreds of NFL players diagnosed with CTE after death

As the latest study found, there have been hundreds of NFL players who, after their brains were studied following their deaths, were diagnosed with CTE. (A 2023 report said that of the 376 former NFL players studied by Boston University’s CTE Center, 345 had been diagnosed with the brain disease.)

Among the most recently diagnosed was former Dallas Cowboys defensive end Marshawn Kneeland , who died by suicide in November following a high-speed chase with police. Boston University researchers analyzed Kneeland’s brain tissue and determined he had Stage 1 CTE.

Aaron Hernandez , whose 2017 death was ruled a suicide, was found to have Stage 3 CTE. He had been in prison at the time of his death in a murder case.

Former Tennessee Titan Frank Wycheck , who died in 2023 after apparently hitting his head in a fall at home, had Stage 3 CTE, his family said. Former NFL Pro Bowl wide receiver Demaryius Thomas had been dealing with depression, anxiety and other CTE symptoms at the time of his 2021 death. His family later confirmed he had Stage 2 CTE.

Irv Cross , a former NFL player turned CBS anchor, was found to have had CTE following his 2021 death. His widow, Liz Cross, told the Associated Press in 2023 that the former Philadelphia Eagles cornerback had experienced depression, mood swings and memory loss that made him not “want to be with people.” Boston University researchers determined Cross had Stage 4 CTE .

Phillip Adams , who spent several seasons in the NFL, fatally shot six people in Rock Hill, South Carolina, before killing himself in 2021. An autopsy later showed he had Stage 2 CTE , Nexstar’s WJZY reported.

Shane Tamura, the man who killed four people in the same New York City building that houses the NFL’s headquarters, was found to have CTE . In a note found on his body, Tamura expressed a grievance with the league – he played football, but never in the NFL – and claimed he suffered from CTE.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Canada slaps retaliatory tariffs on US goods worth $20 billion as trade war intensifies
articles.summary: By Promit Mukherjee and Bhargav Acharya OTTAWA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Canada hit back on Tuesday with retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. ann...
articles.body:
OTTAWA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Canada hit back on Tuesday with retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. annual imports and rolled out aid for businesses and workers, matching Washington's latest ‌duties dollar-for-dollar.

The counter-tariffs on U.S. goods take effect on September 8 and impose duties of 15%, 25% and 50% ‌across around 700 products imported from south of the border, a government statement said.

U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian imports took effect ​on Saturday after talks between the two countries collapsed.

The new tit-for-tat tariffs mark a new low in relations between the longtime allies, and Trump earlier on Tuesday threatened to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles both countries, "Lake America."

"Our dollar-for-dollar, rate for rate counter-tariffs as well as a multi-billion dollar support package will protect workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Canada's Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said.

The White House and the U.S. ‌Trade Representative did not immediately respond to a ⁠request for comment.

Canada levied the 50% tariffs on steel, aluminum, furniture and clothing, set the 25% tariffs on cheese, appliances and some seafood, and placed the 15% tariffs on electronics and tools, a Canadian ⁠government official told reporters.

Trump's new tariffs are relatively narrow, affecting roughly 5% of Canada's exports to the United States. But trade analysts say they could have severe, concentrated effects on some sectors that are already struggling like wood products, particularly kitchen cabinet makers.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs, calculated using ​2024 ​trade figures, cover goods accounting for nearly 4.5% of Canada's imports from ​the United States.

Industry Minister Melanie Joly said the counter-tariffs ‌were primarily aimed at protecting Canadian businesses but were also aimed at applying political pressure before Americans vote in the November 3 midterm elections.

"We need to make sure that the competitors don't have access to the Canadian market in a better way than their own... products, and that's why the retailers need to show that from Canada," she said.

"Second, we're also targeting products that will target states in the U.S. and so we're being wise and strategic to put political pressure, and that's why we think it's ‌the right thing to do right now."

The Canadian tariffs will also cover some ​prepared foods, perfumes and toiletries, plastics, lumber, wood pulp and paper products, ​carpets and clothing.

articles.title: Paxton unveils data center plan, joining other GOP candidates in calling for restrictions
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) unveiled a plan Monday to place restrictions on data centers if elected to the U.S. Senate, becoming the latest GOP candidate to take a stronger stance against the controversial AI infrastructure. Paxton laid out his four-point plan, vowing to “fiercely advocate” for Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) state-level data center…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) unveiled a plan Monday to place restrictions on data centers if elected to the U.S. Senate, becoming the latest GOP candidate to take a stronger stance against the controversial AI infrastructure.

Paxton laid out his four-point plan, vowing to “fiercely advocate” for Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) state-level data center plan and sponsor or back various federal legislation.

This includes legislation that would bar the use of Chinese technology to power data centers and would hold data center developers criminally liable if their infrastructure “empowers AI chatbots that undermine children’s safety.”

He also said he would co-sponsor the Decentralized Access to Technology Alternatives Act, a bill from Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) that would exempt new, off-grid electricity providers from certain federal regulations in an effort to prevent data centers from raising consumer electricity costs.

“My Texas First Data Center Plan will protect our grid, our communities, and our children while ensuring America beats Communist China in the AI race,” Paxton wrote in a post on the social platform X. “Texas First. Always.”

Paxton is facing off against Democratic nominee James Talarico in a tight race for the Texas Senate seat, which the Cook Political Report recently classified as a “toss-up.”

Data centers have increasingly become a central issue in the midterm elections, as Americans have grown wary of the push to rapidly build more of the sprawling server warehouses to support AI development.

This has prompted several Republican candidates to stake out positions against data centers , even as President Trump continues to embrace the build-out.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee for Senate in Michigan, announced last week that he was calling for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction in the state.

In the Pennsylvania governor’s race, Republican Stacy Garrity is calling for a “pause” on data center development and has taken aim at incumbent Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) over his prior support for such projects.

Meanwhile, Abbott announced a series of new restrictions on data centers in June, directing the state’s utility and its regulator to take steps to limit economic impacts on residents. He also pledged to work with the Texas Legislature to mandate water-efficient technologies and repeal data center incentives.

Earlier this month, the Texas governor also said he was placing a moratorium on new data center approvals pending a state audit.
